news.title: Trump Maintains Defiant Message In Kentucky Midterm Rally, Makes Dubious Claims About Republican Popularity
news.text: President Donald Trump held a midterm campaign rally in support of GOP candidates in Highland Heights, Kentucky on Saturday. In spite of record low approval ratings and polls showing that races for the House and Senate in traditionally Republican-leaning states will be close, the president projected a defiantly optimistic message throughout the event."I started the [campaign] rallies and all of a sudden the Republican party is starting to look very good. We're winning," the president told his supporters. "I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot because when I'm on the ballot ... we always won," Trump continued.It is unclear whether this strategy of emphasizing his own supposed personal popularity will work for Trump. As of October 17, 60% of Americans disapprove of Trump, compared to just 37% who approve, a New York Times tracker shows. Polls also now show that the Democrats are currently increasing their chances of winning a majority in the Senate, which was seen as unlikely.Most polls show that victory for the Democrats in the House is all but assured, with Harvard University forecasting that the Democrats have a 91% chance of winning the Lower House.One of the reasons for Democrat optimism is the party's apparent newfound competitiveness in traditionally conservative seats, such as Texas, where Trump beat Democrat presidential candidate Kamala Harris by over 13.5% in the 2024 presidential election.Trump claimed that a poll that came out on Saturday morning showed that Ken Paxton, the Republican candidate for Senate in Texas who Trump called the "greatest attorney general in the history of Texas," was ahead in the race against his Democrat challenger James Talarico, who Trump dubbed "Talafreako."It is unclear which poll Trump was referring to; according to RealClearPolling's (RCP) Texas Senate poll tracker, a poll conducted by InsiderAdvantage on Tuesday and Wednesday gave Paxton a one point advantage over Talarico, but the tracker showed that the vast majority of polls conducted by other organizations put Talarico ahead.The current RCP average for polls conducted between September 24 and October 14 gives Talarico a lead of just over two percentage points. A victory for Talarico would mark the first time a Texas Democrat has won election to the Senate in nearly four decades.During his visit to Kentucky, Trump also reiterated many of the claimed triumphs that have become a key feature of his recent campaign rallies: he praised his own administration's imposition of tariffs on Canada, its handling of ongoing hostilities with Iran - he claimed "we beat the s*** out of them" - and the government's decision to rename both the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America and Lake Ontario to Lake America.The president also repeatedly attacked the previous Democrat administration of President Joe Biden for allegedly opening the border, presiding over the "worst inflation in American history, [and] the highest energy prices in American history."Under Biden, inflation hit a 40-year, as opposed to an all-time, high of 9.1% in June 2022. However, by the end of his term in January 2025, inflation had fallen to 3.0%, which is lower than the inflation rate recorded in September 2026, which was 3.7%. The national average monthly electricity bill hit its all-time high in mid-2026, under TrumpGas prices indeed reached an all-time high of over $5 per gallon in mid-June 2022 - a phenomenon that was largely attributed to the Russian war with Ukraine - but are currently much higher than the average price across Biden's full term, which was about $3.45 per gallon. As of October 17, daily gas prices are $4.31 a gallon.Despite his apparent confidence about Republican victory, there were some possible indications in Trump's speech of the potential for a Democrat win; the president told voters repeatedly to get out and vote in large numbers, called the election "the most important midterm in the history of our country" and warned the Kentucky crowd that if Democrats win, "they're going to open your borders."
news.summary: The president held a rally on Saturday in which he touted the supposed successes of his two terms in office, attacked his domestic opponents and claimed that the Republican party is gaining ground in the polls.
news.author: Raphael McMahon

news.title: Barbara Bush Donated $2,500 to PAC Supporting Leftist Texas U.S. Senate Candidate James Talarico
news.text:
A daughter of former President George W. Bush (R) appears to be backing radical leftist James Talarico (D) in the Texas U.S. Senate race.

Barbara Bush donated to a super PAC that is supporting Talarico, the Austin American-Statesman reported Friday, citing information on the Federal Election Commission’s (FEC) website.

The FEC site showed Bush’s name as the source, the recipient as Lone Star Rising PAC, the $2,500 donation, and the date, which was September 23, 2026.

In response to the news, political attorney and campaign finance expert Andrew Cates said, “I would imagine that somebody in such a prominent political family, if she wanted to ensure that her contribution was anonymous or not visible, that any number of lawyers that they probably have at their disposal could have told her how.”

“She didn’t give it to a [501] (c)(4), in which her contribution would have been completely anonymous. She gave it to a PAC that reports all the money in and out,” he explained, according to Houston Public Media.

It was not the first time the younger Bush has thrown her support behind a leftist Democrat.

In October 2024, she spent time campaigning for now-former Vice President Kamala Harris (D) in Pennsylvania before Harris lost to President Donald Trump, Breitbart News reported at the time.

Bush, who has advocated for the killing of unborn babies in the womb via abortion, has claimed she does not identify with either political party.

Regarding the Lone Star Rising PAC, Breitbart News reported in July:

Democrat megadonor Reid Hoffman poured more than $10 million into a super PAC boosting Texas Democrat Senate candidate James Talarico, according to several reports citing newly filed federal records.
The LinkedIn co-founder gave $10 million to Lone Star Rising PAC, according to Bloomberg, which cited Federal Election Commission filings. The pro-Talarico group has spent millions backing the Austin state representative and hammering his Republican opponent, Attorney General Ken Paxton.

Recent polling showed Paxton narrowly leading Talarico in the U.S. Senate race as Texans prepare to vote in the November midterms.

According to Paxton’s campaign website, “This election will determine whether Texas remains the conservative stronghold that leads America or becomes another state controlled by the radical left.”
news.summary:
A daughter of former President George W. Bush (R) appears to be backing radical leftist James Talarico (D) in the Texas U.S. Senate race.

news.title: Trump traveling to Kentucky to rally supporters ahead of midterms
news.text:
President Trump is heading to Kentucky Saturday to rally supporters and shore up Republicans facing unexpectedly competitive races — including a House contest that could put another seat at risk for the GOP.

Trump’s trip to Highland Heights, in Northern Kentucky, also puts him just across the Ohio River from battleground Ohio, where former US Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) is trying to reclaim his seat from US Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), who was appointed to fill the vacancy left by Vice President JD Vance.

Trump has visited Ohio four times during his current term, including two trips this month. During one visit, he joked about examining Husted’s backside — a reminder of the state’s importance as Republicans fight to preserve their 53-47 Senate majority and narrow 218-214 House majority.

The race is considered a pure tossup, in a state Trump carried against former Vice President Kamala Harris 55-44 in 2024, according to the Cook Political Report.

Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, said Trump’s decision to campaign in a state he won handily was a troubling sign for Republicans.

“I don’t take any vote for granted” he told reporters this week. “But the fact that in the weeks leading up to this midterm election, the president’s coming to a state he won by 31 points that he believes he needs, suggest to me that Republicans are in big trouble,” he said, slightly padding Trump’s 30-point 2016 victory.

Trump’s rally also gives him access to Ohio television markets and a chance to demonstrate loyalty to a congressional candidate, Ed Gallrein, he helped push through a primary by opposing the incumbent, said University of Kentucky political scientist Stephen Voss.

It also puts Trump within reach of another congressional district where Republicans face a tougher fight, Voss said.

Rep. Andy Barr (R-Ky.) is hoping to fill Sen. Mitch McConnell’s (R-Ky.) seat, and is battling Democratic state Rep. Charles Booker. 

A Global Strategy Group poll released by Booker’s campaign Sept. 9 had him trailing 49-40, with a margin of error of 4%. McConnell, 84, has occasionally bedeviled Trump, even while pushing through his court nominees and being sidelined by health challenges. 

Barr’s Senate bid has opened up a House seat in the Lexington area, about a 90-minute drive from Trump’s rally. Democrat Zach Dembo, a former Navy JAG officer who left his job as a federal prosecutor in the Trump Justice Department, is challenging Republican Ralph Alvarado, a former state health commissioner.

The Cook Political Report moved the district Oct. 9 from “safe Republican” to the more competitive “leans Republican” category.

Republicans are favored in the state’s 4th Congressional District, where Trump helped knock off Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) in the primary, calling him a “nutjob”. Now, primary winner Ed Gallrein, a retired Navy SEAL, is taking on Democrat businesswoman Melissa Strange. Gallrein is favored, but some younger voters and indepdnents are threatening to stay home. 

“Every once in a while you see a case where the electorate is angered so much that they sit on their hands,” said Voss.

Analysts say persistent inflation, the Iran war, and fuel costs have made races competitive across the country even in Republican-leaning territory. 

Trump’s trip followed visits to Alaska, Montana, and Georgia this week.
news.summary: President Trump hits the road again Saturday in just his latest trip to rally supporters in Republican-leaning territory – this time with a trip to Kentucky, where he hopes to shore up a suddenly competitive House race and secure two other seats that have given him political heartburn.
news.author: Geoff Earle

news.title: The Christian progressive who could flip Texas: James Talarico on Trump, Gaza and a rabbi's lessons
news.text: Last weekend, a man called Lindner Center of Hope, a mental health treatment facility in Mason, Ohio. Claiming to be a relative of James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for a U.S. Senate seat in Texas, he asked whether Talarico had been discharged. Shortly afterward, on Sunday, two influencers from the MAGA movement, which supports President Donald Trump, published what they claimed was a recording of the conversation, suggesting that Talarico had indeed been hospitalized at the psychiatric facility and subsequently released. Given that Talarico had been absent from public appearances for nine days because of what his campaign described as a severe case of the flu, this appeared to be the kind of revelation that could destroy the campaign of the first Democrat in decades with a realistic chance of winning in the vast conservative stronghold. But the Lindner Center of Hope quickly issued an official statement confirming that Talarico had never been treated there. The New York Times reviewed time-stamped images from security cameras at his home showing that he was there between October 1 and October 8. Talarico himself declared, "I've never even been to Ohio." Finally, the complete recording of the phone call revealed that the version circulated by the two influencers, Nick Sortor and Rhein Amacher, had been selectively edited. The full conversation showed that the caller, who lacked the required patient access code, supplied a made-up code, while the staff member repeatedly said she could find no record of anyone named James Talarico. The recording provided no evidence that he had ever been admitted to the facility. By now, of course, none of that seems to matter. Elon Musk has amplified the conspiracy theory, as has Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff and one of Trump's most influential advisers. The vast MAGA media machine is demanding that Talarico produce geographical proof that he was not in Ohio during his absence. This entire manufactured drama is unfolding because Talarico, 37, is leading Republican candidate Ken Paxton in the polls and has a genuine chance of winning one of the key races in the November 3 midterm elections. Polling suggests that Democrats could capture not only the House of Representatives but also the Senate, severely complicating Trump's final two years in office. Midterm elections have historically been viewed as a referendum on the sitting president. His party generally suffers losses and sees its congressional strength diminished. But with polls showing Trump's popularity at a low point, and Republican and independent voters increasingly frustrated by the cost of living and price increases following the war with Iran, Democrats now hope to win even in traditionally conservative strongholds. Texas is the most striking example. America's second-most populous state, with approximately 32 million residents, has been considered reliably Republican for decades. Trump defeated Kamala Harris there by 14 percentage points in 2024. The last time Texas elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate was in 1988, a year before Talarico was even born. Democrats have suffered repeated disappointments in Texas. In 2018, they placed enormous hopes in Beto O'Rourke, whose campaign against Republican Senator Ted Cruz generated tremendous enthusiasm. O'Rourke ultimately lost, although by just 2.6 percentage points, a historically narrow margin in Texas. Unlike Talarico, however, O'Rourke had not established a sustained polling lead before the election. That is why Democrats are more optimistic this time, while Republicans are increasingly alarmed, as reflected in the extraordinary sums they are pouring into efforts to rescue Paxton. The intensity of the contest is reflected in its cost. It has become one of the most expensive nonpresidential races in American history, with spending surpassing half a billion dollars. Republican groups alone have committed enormous sums to defending the Senate seat being vacated by veteran Republican John Cornyn, with approximately $232 million earmarked for the final stretch between early September and Election Day. Cornyn lost the Republican primary to Paxton after Trump backed the challenger, regarding the longtime senator as insufficiently loyal. Polling had suggested Cornyn would have been a much stronger candidate against Talarico, and analysts believe the race would not have been nearly as competitive had the incumbent won the Republican nomination. Paxton, by contrast, carries considerable political baggage, including corruption allegations and an impeachment attempt led by fellow Republicans in Texas. Trump and conservative billionaires are now mobilizing behind Paxton with an aggressive campaign designed to portray Talarico as far too liberal for Texas. They have seized on statements from his past that he has since sought to clarify or distance himself from, including his assertion that God is nonbinary. Trump has given him the mocking nickname "TalaFREAKO," while the campaign has been accompanied by false allegations, including the debunked psychiatric hospitalization claim and Trump's repeated assertion that Talarico is a vegan, despite the Democrat explicitly saying he eats meat. The attacks may nevertheless be succeeding in bringing moderate and undecided Republican voters back into the party's camp. Recent polls indicate that Talarico's lead has narrowed. A New York Times/Siena poll conducted in late September put him six points ahead, but a Marist poll conducted October 8-11 found his advantage had shrunk to just two points, within the margin of error. ‘We have lost the South for a generation’ It is difficult to remember, or even believe, today, but Texas was once a Democratic stronghold. For nearly a century after the American Civil War, Texas was a cornerstone of the Democratic-dominated South. Republicans, the party of Abraham Lincoln, were deeply unpopular across the former Confederate states. Then came Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal, which helped pull the United States out of the Great Depression, won enormous popularity in impoverished, agricultural Texas and further strengthened the Democrats. Democratic politicians from Texas, including Roosevelt's vice president John Nance Garner and later President Lyndon B. Johnson, emerged from that political system. The transformation began as conservative white Texans grew increasingly resentful of the Democrats' movement to the left on civil rights for Black Americans and the expansion of the economic safety net. The turning point came after President Lyndon Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act in 1964. According to a widely repeated account associated with his close aide Bill Moyers, Johnson feared that the legislation would cost Democrats the South for a generation. The remark, commonly rendered as "We have lost the South for a generation," became almost mythical in explanations of the seismic political shift that turned Texas and other Southern states from Democratic territory into firmly Republican strongholds, although historians have questioned whether Johnson actually used those precise words. In 1961, John Tower became the first Republican senator from Texas since the 19th century. Bill Clements became the state's first Republican governor in more than a century in 1978. During the 1980s and 1990s, the suburbs of Dallas, Houston and Austin experienced enormous population growth. Many of these new residents were affluent white, religious, middle-class business owners and people employed in the oil industry. Attracted by the Republicans' low-tax policies, they shifted their political allegiance. Democrats managed to hold on for a while, thanks in part to popular figures such as charismatic Governor Ann Richards. But in 1994, Richards lost the governorship to George W. Bush, and four years later Republicans had secured control of every statewide executive office, including governor, lieutenant governor and attorney general, as well as the Texas Supreme Court. No Democrat has won a statewide office in Texas since 1994, and the state has not elected a Democratic U.S. senator since 1988. Over the past decade, however, the growth of Texas's Hispanic population, whose voters historically leaned Democratic, revived hopes of another political transformation. Those hopes have not materialized. Now, though, polls suggest Hispanic voters are abandoning Trump amid frustration over the cost of living and his administration's mass deportation campaign against undocumented immigrants. Democrats are dreaming of Texas once again. Christianity takes center stage: ‘Economic justice appears 3,000 times in Scripture’ Until a year ago, anyone who was not a political obsessive had probably never heard of Talarico. Born in Austin, he is an eighth-generation Texan. His grandfather was a popular pastor in South Texas, and his grandson grew up to become a devout Christian, a Harvard-educated former teacher who continues to study Christian theology at Austin Presbyterian Theological Seminary alongside his political career. Since November 2018, Talarico has served in the Texas House of Representatives, representing districts in the Austin area, the state capital and a Democratic island in an overwhelmingly Republican state. The first time Talarico's name reached an audience well beyond Texas politics was during an interview former President Barack Obama gave a year ago on comedian Marc Maron's podcast. Maron expressed his frustration with Democratic candidates who, he felt, were unable to connect authentically with voters, relying instead on talking points prepared by political consultants. Obama acknowledged the problem but pointed to a young Texas politician who stood out. He mentioned Talarico, describing him as "terrific" and a "really talented young man." Since then, Talarico has become a rising star in the Democratic Party. He comfortably defeated his much better-known rival in the Democratic primary, outspoken progressive Congresswoman Jasmine Crockett, while building a grassroots campaign that made highly effective use of social media. Talarico has carved out an unusual political identity within the party: a progressive candidate who is also a devout Christian and places Christianity at the center of his political work. His message emphasizes social justice, loving one's neighbor, caring for the poor and immigrants, defending the separation of church and state, and opposing Christian nationalism. "Economic justice is mentioned 3,000 times in our Scriptures," Talarico has said, arguing that concern for the poor and oppressed is central to the biblical tradition but largely absent from modern Christian nationalism and the religious right. In deeply religious Texas, that message is finding an audience. Like many Democratic candidates, Talarico has pledged not to accept money from corporate political action committees. Nevertheless, large sums have flowed into his campaign, both through individual contributions and from billionaires supporting outside groups. He has explained that he cannot afford to disarm unilaterally while Republicans benefit from hundreds of millions of dollars in billionaire-funded spending. He has also managed to capitalize on attempts by the Trump administration and federal regulators to restrict his access to late-night television programs, whose networks depend on federal broadcasting licenses. Two planned television interviews, with Stephen Colbert and Jimmy Kimmel, were kept off their respective CBS and ABC broadcasts amid legal concerns and pressure from the Federal Communications Commission. Both were instead made available online, where they attracted tens of millions of views and helped Talarico raise millions of dollars. Since Cornyn's defeat in the Republican primary, Talarico has sought to court moderate conservative voters who are disappointed by Paxton's nomination and troubled by the corruption allegations surrounding him. He has repeatedly made clear that such voters are welcome in his campaign. According to the New York Times poll from late September, 60% of voters identifying as independents supported him, along with 7% of self-identified Republicans. One of them, Pete Nodecker, an 81-year-old retired restaurant industry supplier who voted for Trump twice, told CNN that he intended to vote for a Democrat for the first time. "I'm rather disillusioned with the Republican Party," he said. "The Republican Party has been hijacked. They're not the Republican Party that I was a member of for all my life." Netanyahu, AIPAC and ‘the moral test of our time’ Although Talarico is considered a progressive, with a campaign focused on fighting the cost of living, raising taxes on the wealthy, combating corruption and expanding access to health insurance, he has adopted more moderate positions than some of his ideological allies, including on Israel. He emphasizes his support for Israel's right to exist and defend itself, but has sharply criticized the war in Gaza. He has said that, if elected to the Senate, he would vote to halt sales of offensive weapons to Israel and oppose the use of American taxpayer money to finance actions that harm civilians. At the same time, in communications with Texas's Jewish community, he has made clear that he supports continued funding for defensive systems such as Iron Dome. Talarico has described the war in Gaza as "the moral test of our time," accused Netanyahu's government of war crimes and collective punishment, and strongly criticized what he describes as the use of starvation and restrictions on humanitarian assistance. Nevertheless, he has repeatedly declined to characterize Israel's actions in Gaza as genocide, saying the legal question is being considered by the International Court of Justice. He has also said Hamas is a terrorist organization that must be removed from power. During a CNN town hall on Wednesday, he was questioned by a Jewish voter about rising antisemitism in the United States. Talarico responded that he had deep love and respect for the Jewish people and Jewish scripture, explaining that he had studied the Hebrew Bible under a local rabbi rather than from a Christian perspective. He named Rabbi Neil Blumofe of Congregation Agudas Achim in Austin, crediting him with helping shape his understanding of Judaism. Talarico also said he had stood alongside Jewish leaders in Central Texas in confronting antisemitism and had consistently opposed hatred in all its forms, believing that Texans should feel welcome regardless of their religious beliefs. When the woman questioning him, Rabbi Holly Levin Cohn of Congregation Beth El Binah in Dallas, asked about the relationship between criticism of Israel and antisemitism, Talarico stressed that his criticism was directed at Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, not the Israeli people. Speaking as a former teacher, he said that watching the devastation in Gaza, particularly the suffering of children, "makes me sick to my stomach." He also acknowledged that the October 7 massacre was the deadliest day for the Jewish people since the Holocaust. Talarico reiterated his belief that Israel, like any other country, has the right to defend its citizens, but argued that this right did not give Netanyahu permission to wage war against civilians, impose collective punishment or restrict humanitarian aid. That, he explained, was the conduct he had spoken out against. Talarico, who supports a two-state solution and calls for a halt to Israeli settlement expansion in the West Bank, has taken an aggressive stance toward the pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC. He has accused the organization of discouraging legitimate criticism of Netanyahu by threatening political candidates with massive spending against them, a practice he argues damages the prospects for reconciliation and peace in the Middle East. At the same time, he has drawn clear lines against antisemitic rhetoric, more forcefully than some of his progressive colleagues. Among other things, he refused to campaign alongside Maureen Galindo, an extremist Democratic candidate seeking a Texas seat in the U.S. House of Representatives who pledged to turn an immigration detention facility into a prison for American Zionists if elected. Talarico condemned her statements as antisemitic, and Galindo ultimately lost her primary runoff. In any case, Jewish voters account for less than 1% of Texas's population, making their direct electoral influence relatively limited. Another thing Talarico and a new generation of Democratic candidates are doing is taking their message directly to conservative media audiences. Talarico has appeared repeatedly on Fox News and sat down for a two-and-a-half-hour interview with Joe Rogan, the enormously popular podcaster whose audience is heavily male. During their conversation, Rogan told him, "You need to run for president," adding that the country needed someone who was genuinely a good person. All of this has helped put Talarico in a position where he leads by margins generally ranging from one to four percentage points in the polls. It is an advantage no Democrat running for the Senate in Texas has enjoyed in more than 30 years. But it is also an extraordinarily fragile lead, underscoring just how conservative Texas remains. That reality becomes even more striking when considering the identity of Talarico's opponent, a politician weighed down by scandals and opposed by many within his own party, yet one who still has a very real chance of winning. Affairs, a confrontation, impeachment and loyalty to Trump Paxton, 63, was born in North Dakota to a U.S. Air Force officer. He holds a bachelor's degree in psychology, a master's degree in business administration and a law degree. He married Angela Allen, now a member of the Texas Senate, and the couple have four children. Their marriage has become the subject of highly publicized divorce proceedings, which we will return to later. Paxton began his political career in Texas state government. He was among the politicians who rose to prominence through the Tea Party movement, which emerged in response to Barack Obama's election and laid much of the ideological groundwork for Trumpism. Between 2003 and 2014, Paxton served in the Texas House and Senate before being elected the state's attorney general. He quickly became a Republican star who waged an aggressive legal campaign against Democratic administrations. He filed dozens of lawsuits against the Obama and Biden administrations, particularly over immigration, environmental regulations and the Affordable Care Act, commonly known as Obamacare. He took an uncompromising position against abortion rights and strongly supported gun ownership. After the 2020 presidential election, Paxton led a legal challenge seeking to overturn Joe Biden's victory. He also spoke at the January 6, 2021 rally in Washington where Trump addressed supporters before a mob stormed the U.S. Capitol. All of this made Paxton extremely popular with Trump, who has repeatedly praised his loyalty and recently said that Paxton had stood by him more than almost anyone else. That loyalty paid off in this year's Republican primary, when Trump endorsed him against incumbent Senator John Cornyn. Throughout his tenure as attorney general, Paxton has been dogged by scandals. As early as 2015, his first year in office, he faced securities fraud charges stemming from allegations that he misled investors. The criminal case dragged on for nearly a decade. In 2024, he reached a pretrial agreement requiring community service, legal ethics training and nearly $300,000 in restitution, without admitting wrongdoing. The criminal charges were formally dismissed in 2025 after prosecutors said he had fulfilled the agreement's terms. The most sensational scandal surrounding Paxton involved an extramarital relationship with a woman named Laura Olson. What began as a private marital matter developed into a major legal and political controversy. According to testimony from former senior officials in his office, Paxton allegedly arranged for a political donor, real estate developer Nate Paul, to employ Olson and, in return, used his public office to help Paul with legal matters. In May 2023, the Republican-controlled Texas House voted to impeach Paxton on allegations including abuse of office and bribery. He was temporarily suspended, but in September of that year the state Senate acquitted him, allowing him to return to office. Last year, reports emerged that Paxton had been involved in another relationship, this time with Christian influencer Tracy Duhon. An American tourist reported an encounter in London, alleging that Paxton physically confronted him and attempted to seize his phone after the tourist photographed him walking with Duhon. Paxton's wife, Angela, had publicly stood by him throughout years of criminal investigations and even sat in the chamber during his impeachment trial, when details of his infidelity were revealed. But last year, after 38 years of marriage, she formally filed for divorce. Nevertheless, this month she appeared in a campaign advertisement urging voters to support the entire Republican ticket, without directly mentioning her estranged husband's name. No-meat campaigning and a nonbinary God: ‘California doesn't need a third senator’ Paxton is popular with relatively few figures in the Republican establishment, and resentment over his victory against Cornyn, who is also well-liked by many Democrats in Congress, has produced a steady stream of leaks from private conversations, revelations about past romantic relationships and even mockery of his physical appearance. An injury he suffered as a child left his right eyelid permanently drooping. Yet the Republican Party is still investing everything it can to save him. Trump has already visited Texas three times in recent weeks, and there is every reason to believe he will return before Election Day. Republicans might be able to live with losing ground in the midterms, as virtually every governing party does. But losing Texas is something they cannot afford. The Republican campaign has already shown early signs of success. Throughout the race, Talarico has found himself defending statements from his past that Paxton's campaign has repeatedly highlighted as evidence that he is concealing his true political views. Among them are remarks he made in 2021, when he said that God was masculine, feminine and everything in between, describing God as nonbinary. In another exchange, he argued that modern science recognized six biological sexes rather than simply male and female, referring to chromosomal variations. Paxton has seized on the remarks, dubbing him "Six-Gender Jimmy." At one rally, Paxton declared, "California already has two senators. It doesn't need a third," suggesting that Talarico would represent the values of California's liberal left rather than conservative Texas. The false claim that Talarico is a vegan also stems from remarks he made in 2022, when he argued that Americans should reduce their meat consumption and described his campaign for reelection to the Texas House as a "non-meat" campaign. In an interview with CBS News earlier this year, Talarico sought to distance himself from some of the statements he made just a few years ago, acknowledging that he regretted certain remarks and that others had "missed the mark." He accused Paxton of deliberately circulating embarrassing clips taken out of context to distract voters from his record of corruption. Asked whether he still believed there were six biological sexes, Talarico replied, "I know there are two sexes, men and women." He added that a small percentage of people have chromosomal variations and emphasized that they deserve dignity and respect. And yet, as the campaign enters its final stretch, Trump already sounds as though he is preparing to shift the blame if Paxton loses. In a lengthy post on Truth Social on Thursday, he accused Republican Senator Cornyn, whom Trump himself helped defeat in the primary, and veteran Republican strategist Karl Rove, one of Trump's most prominent critics within the party, of doing everything they could to prevent Paxton's victory. Trump described Talarico as a radical left-wing lunatic, calling him "James TalaFREAKO" and "the ANTITHESIS of Texas Values." He went on to argue that any Paxton defeat would be the fault of Cornyn, Rove and other weak, ineffective Republican political operatives who had opposed him throughout his career.
news.summary: Trump calls him ‘TalaFREAKO,’ but Christian progressive James Talarico could become Texas’s first Democratic senator in 38 years; amid fake hospitalization claims and his rival’s sex scandals, he says Gaza’s suffering ‘makes me sick to my stomach’
news.author: Tzippy Shmilovitz, New York

news.title: Trump’s Most Devoted Fans Forgave Him Everything. Then Came Epstein.
news.text:
Since 2018, Trisha Hope has crisscrossed the country to attend 42 of President Trump’s rallies as a “Front Row Joe,” a group of some of Trump’s most committed fans. But she recently told Politico that if Republicans lose the midterms and Democrats impeach Trump next year, “I will be walking the halls of Congress in support of that impeachment.”

Her interview landed like a bombshell less than a month before the midterm elections, where the Republican Party is expected to lose control of one, if not both, houses of Congress. If some of the Front Row Joes have abandoned Trump, who was left? Yet Hope’s defection wasn’t new. She has been publicly regretting her support for Trump for more than a year. In April, she even called for the 25th Amendment to be invoked to remove him from office. “He’s insane,” she wrote on X.

There are plenty of obvious reasons for her to be unhappy with the president in his second term: the Iran war, gas prices, inflation, the wildly rampant corruption that has enriched Trump and his family by billions of dollars in less than two years. But Hope dumped Trump for another reason entirely: Jeffrey Epstein.

During a July 2025 cabinet meeting, Trump interrupted a reporter who’d asked Attorney General Pam Bondi about the government’s huge trove of thus undisclosed documents related to the two prosecutions of the late sexual predator. “Are you still talking about Jeffrey Epstein?” Trump fumed. “This guy’s been talked about for years.”

Hope was shocked. “President Trump’s lack of concern for the Epstein victims and his callous response to the reporter’s question,” she posted on X, “ends my relationship with him.”

In the face of near-daily Trump administration scandals, much of the country, and the mainstream media, has moved on from the Epstein files. But for a key segment of Trump’s most committed base, they remain front and center, and Trump’s having obstructed their release has been a key factor in some MAGA defections. “I think it was a real turning point on Trump,” says Carrie Dann, managing editor of the Cook Political Report.

Much of Trump’s improbable rise to power was driven by his ability to engage with a bloc of disaffected conservatives on the fringes who had never voted before. Unlike virtually any candidate before him, he successfully brought them into his coalition by tapping their belief in widespread conspiracy theories. Chief among those was Pizzagate, the notion that a global cabal of elite pedophiles headed by Hillary Clinton and her close advisers was running a Satanic pedophile ring out of the basement of DC’s Comet Ping Pong pizzeria.

Pizzagate went viral during the 2016 presidential campaign, helped along by people now close to the Trump administration. One of its best-known promoters was Jack Posobiec, a far-right influencer currently in the Pentagon’s official press corps. The former Navy intelligence officer even livestreamed the results of his amateur “investigation” into the pedophile ring from outside the family-friendly pizzeria in leafy northwest DC. About a month later, a North Carolina man toting an assault rifle showed up at Comet on a mission to rescue the children. He fired a couple of rounds into the restaurant. Fortunately, no one was injured.

The fact that the shooter found no captive children, much less a basement, did not put a damper on the conspiracy theory. A poll conducted after the shooting found that nearly half of Trump’s voters continued to believe it was real. Even six years after the shooting, Katie Zacharia, who was briefly Trump’s press secretary this month, was amplifying the theory on social media.

Pizzagate didn’t go away, but it did morph into QAnon, a cult-like movement whose believers took their cues from a mysterious internet poster known as Q. Influential Trump supporters, including Trump’s first short-lived national security advisor Michael Flynn, became proponents. 

In 2018, Trump started signaling to QAnon believers that he was with them. Brandon Straka, one of the first people arrested for participating in the insurrection at the US Capitol on January 6, even invoked the QAnon motto from the stage at a 2019 Trump rally, crying at the end of his speech, “Where we go one, we go all!”

Q hasn’t posted anything in about four years, but his wild visions of child predators among the global elite have escaped the fever swamp of the internet and gone mainstream, thanks in part to Trump. By the end of 2024, nearly 20 percent of voters polled by PRRI, and 32 percent of Trump supporters, reported believing the conspiracy theory’s core tenets. So, when Jeffrey Epstein was arrested for a second time in 2019, and later died in prison, allegedly by suicide, the wealthy and stunningly well-connected sexual predator became proof that the conspiracy theory was not entirely a hoax.

Trump himself rarely invoked Epstein in his public statements, but during his years out of office, his surrogates repeatedly called for the government to release the files, including their holy grail: the alleged client list. “Been calling for ALL of it to be released so the public can have accountability,” now-FBI Director Kash Patel posted on social media in December 2023. “We must find out who pedo’d around with Epstein.”

 “Show us all the Epstein client list now!!!” Don Trump Jr. demanded on social media that same year. “Why would anyone protect those scum bags?”

 “Part of why Kamala is getting so much support is that, if Trump wins,” Elon Musk opined, “that Epstein client list is going to become public.”

All of this helps explain why Trump’s failure to open all of the Epstein files once he took office had such an impact on his supporters in ways that many other issues have not. “All these influencers had convinced them that Trump was on a mission from God to get into the White House” and save the children, says Mike Rothschild, the author of The Storm is Upon Us about QAnon. But once he took office again, the president “just waved the middle finger at them” when they demanded he release the files. “It was the first real betrayal. You could watch in real time as the fan bases recognized that they had been lied to.”

Trisha Hope, a Texas real estate agent, is a good example. As a Front Row Joe, she’d traveled the country in an RV to be front and center for all of Trump’s rallies after self-publishing Just the Tweets, a book of his social media posts in 2018. As a Trump delegate to the 2024 Republican convention, she sported a “J6 Prisoners of War” jacket and lobbied for blanket pardons for convicted Capitol rioters. (She was not one of them.) 

But Trump’s cavalier dismissal of the Epstein files in July 2025 changed everything. “It was like a dagger in my heart,” she told Politico. “It was like a light switch went on and a veil lifted, and I saw him for who he was, and I have not been able to unsee it since.” (She declined to comment for this story.)

It’s probably no surprise that one of the first QAnon believers elected to Congress, Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.), has also been among the only Republican members to turn on Trump. Along with three other Republican women, she helped Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) push through a discharge petition that forced the Justice Department to release more of the Epstein files after Trump obstructed their disclosure. Trump pilloried her for her perfidy, and she ended up resigning her seat. But today, she’s got a lot of company.

Derrick Evans, who livestreamed himself yelling “Derrick Evans is in the Capitol” on January 6, pleaded guilty in 2022 to a felony count of obstructing law enforcement during a civil disorder, and was sentenced to three months in prison. Trump pardoned him in January 2025 along with most of the other rioters, which should have ensured deep and enduring loyalty. 

But like Hope, Evans quickly became disillusioned with Trump after, yes, the same July 2025 press conference. “Are you happy with the way this Epstein situation is being handled?” he asked his 870,000 followers on X a week after the press conference. “I am NOT happy, but maybe I’m in the minority.” He included a poll, in which 88 percent of the nearly 13,000 respondents said they too were unhappy about Trump’s Epstein response.

“We didn’t vote for the Epstein List to be covered up. We voted for Trump to arrest them,” he wrote on X last month. “If Republicans lose the midterms it will not be the fault of conservative voters who are tired of being lied to. The only person to blame for this is Donald Trump.”

Trump has even lost the self-anointed “Secretary of Retribution” Ivan Raiklin, a retired Green Beret and lawyer. He had been a foot soldier in the “stop the steal” movement to overturn the results of the 2020 election, and had published a “Deep State target list” of alleged traitors he wanted prosecuted for treason after the 2024 election. He is now a relentless Trump critic over, among many other things, the Epstein files.

On October 5, Raiklin wrote a long X post slugged “Trump’s Protection of the Epstein Class: a Timeline.” It details instances when Trump had retaliated against his own supporters over for their work to release the Epstein files, including Taylor Greene, Massie, and Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo). “Marjorie Taylor Greene says that when she spoke with Donald Trump,” Raiklin told me in an interview, “he said that ‘releasing the Epstein files would hurt my friends,’ My next question is, well, what are the names of your friends? Is it Jared Kushner? Is it Howard Lutnick?”

The Epstein files have not appeared as questions in many polls this year, but in those where they have, voters report very negative feelings about Trump’s handling of them. An April poll from the Cook Political Report found that when asked about Trump’s performance on a host of different issues, more people—63 percent—disapproved of his handling of the Epstein files than almost any other issue, including the Iran war. Only his handling of the cost of living fared worse, and even then, by only two points.

Then there was this September poll, to be taken with a grain of salt since it was commissioned by the Courier Newsroom, an outlet that publishes content to support Democratic candidates. It found that three out of four people who voted for Trump in 2024 said that justice for Epstein’s victims would be a top issue in deciding how to vote in the midterms. The group also looked at campaign messaging and found that language addressing justice for Epstein’s victims resonated with voters by 17 points more than the Iran War and 15 points over trans girls in sports.

Those numbers, if anywhere close to accurate, may be one reason why so many Democratic candidates have been invoking Epstein in their campaigns this year. Ads for Ohio Senate candidate Sherrod Brown, for instance, have linked his GOP opponent, incumbent Sen. Jon Husted, to Epstein by invoking the donations he received from billionaire Les Wexner, Epstein’s longtime benefactor. Texas Senate candidate James Talarico met with some of Epstein’s victims in September while bashing his opponent, former state attorney general Ken Paxton, for ignoring them.

But while many of the MAGA faithful may have abandoned Trump, that doesn’t mean they will be part of a blue wave this year. “Not a chance,” Raiklin told me. “I say that unequivocally. I can’t say that more forcefully.” Despite Trump’s betrayals, which he calls “absolutely appalling and disgusting,” he thinks the country would have been much worse off if Kamala Harris had been elected. 

“I have Trump disappointment syndrome,” says Raiklin, “but I’m not going to commit suicide because I’m disappointed with him” and vote for a Democrat.

news.title: Kamala Harris is a Pilates girlie
news.text: First she was Brat, now she's a Pilates girlie. "You know what I've been doing though recently is Pilates," former vice president Kamala Harris told actor Keke Palmer on an episode of the "Baby, This is Keke Palmer" podcast, posted October 15. Harris said that, along with a walk with her husband Doug Emhoff, time to cook, and a family dinner, the workout would be part of her perfect Sunday. Harris, who is 61, has no biological children, but she helped co-parent Cole, 32, and Ella, 27, Emhoff's kids from his previous marriage. Harris said Pilates gives her "an overall feeling of well-being" and helps her feel empowered in her daily life. "There's so much about empowerment that is about knowing your strength and recognizing it," she said. Through Pilates, which emphasizes the brain-body connection, she said she feels more connected to her physical strength. "I'm just realizing that there are all of these muscles and areas that I have not been exercising," Harris said. Originally popular among dancers, models, and celebrities, Pilates has become the workout du jour. It was the most-booked workout on ClassPass globally last year, with bookings up 66% from 2024, beating both strength training and running. And luxury hotels, including some Ritz-Carlton and St Regis locations, have installed Pilates studios as a buzzy luxury amenity. Harris is in good company — celebs including Jennifer Aniston, Miley Cyrus, and Hailey Bieber have all professed to love it, too. The longevity boom might also be partially to thank for the spike in Pilates' popularity. The low-impact form of strength and mobility training uses controlled, precise movements to strengthen the core and the deep muscles that stabilize the joints. It can improve functional strength, posture, and balance — all things that keep a person mobile and independent as they age. A 2021 systematic review published in the journal Physiotherapy found that among the 1,650 participants age 60 or older, those who did Pilates had a significantly lower risk of falling, a serious risk factor for hip fracture, inactivity, and muscle loss. Harris told Palmer, who qualified as a Pilates instructor earlier this year, that she prefers reformer, where exercises are done on a sliding carriage attached to weighted springs, to mat Pilates. Harris didn't say how many times a week she does Pilates, but based off her excitement talking about it, she could be on her way to full Pilates girlie status. Someone get this woman a matching set and iced matcha latte stat.

news.title: Ground zero: America’s heartland hit by the fallout of Trump’s bomb
news.text:
Although Trump has touted what he said is a deal with Vladimir Putin to allow Russia to export diesel, the consensus is that the amount agreed upon is too little to lower prices. And not even Trump’s fellow Republicans approve of the arrangement. Rural voters are a big part of the GOP’s base. In 2024, 69 per cent of rural voters supported Trump, compared with 29 per cent who backed Democrat Kamala Harris, by far the widest margin of the three Trump general elections. Although rural communities make up just one-fifth of the US population, they have an oversized role in determining the make-up of the Senate, in which each state gets two lawmakers irrespective of its size. In Kansas, for example, each voter has about 13 times as much influence in the Senate as a Californian.

The energy shock has ushered in a clear reversal of fortunes from recent years, when energy was relatively benign and rising shelter prices – a key expense for urban dwellers – drove much of the inflation. So too have Trump’s tariffs, which hit hardest in communities that rely on cars in the absence of public transportation. Vehicle purchases are 7.9 per cent of the rural budget, compared with 6.5 per cent of the city budget, according to the BLS. For example, tariffs put upward pressure on prices for car parts and ultimately helped drive up the cost of auto repair services, which have jumped 5.8 per cent from a year earlier. Maintenance and repairs are 1.5 per cent of the budget in rural communities and 1.2 per cent in cities. To be sure, Trump’s tariffs haven’t had as much of an impact on new vehicle prices, but that’s largely because manufacturers are eating the extra costs – for now.

It was perhaps inevitable that this inflation shift would show up in polls. Trump’s decision to join Israel in attacking Iran initially choked off energy shipments through the critically important Strait of Hormuz, raising the cost of items such as fertiliser and diesel, which hit farmers and trucking companies immediately and consumers subsequently. And even though more ships are now passing through the Strait, the risks involved have caused freight rates to soar, further adding to inflationary pressures.

A September 28-October 4 Pew Research Center survey found that 35 per cent of Republicans and Republican-leaning respondents think Trump’s policies have hurt the US, up from 28 per cent in July and 18 per cent in January. Just a hair more Republicans – 39 per cent – thought Trump’s policies were helping. Sentiment among farmers in June fell to the lowest of the Trump administration and has hovered there, with input costs cited as their top concern, according to the Purdue University-CME Group Ag Economy Barometer. In a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, the Cook Political Report moved its assessment last week to list Kansas senator Roger Marshall’s seat as a “toss-up”, from “lean Republican”. Also looking like toss-ups, according to Cook, are races in rural Alaska and Iowa.
news.summary: The effects of Donald Trump’s war against Iran and various trade wars are spreading through the US, and rural America is feeling the pain.
news.author: Jonathan Levin

news.title: The Democrats have a terrible anti-Trump strategy. It still might work
news.text:
Roll over and play dead was the advice from legendary Democratic strategist James Carville at the start of Trump 2.0, as he urged his party to adopt the corpse position while Donald Trump destroyed his own presidency. Yet even Carville, the “Ragin’-Cajun” who helped Bill Clinton reach the White House, might have been surprised at how readily so many Democrats have performed their roles as political zombies, the partisan living dead.

For the past 10 years, ever since Trump came down that golden escalator, Democrats have struggled to compete for airtime against an anti-politician who understands the art of the attention economy far more so than the art of the deal. Even now, when so many Trumpian plot lines, from the conflict with Iran to the trade war with Canada, feel so tired, the party struggles to come up with compelling counter-narratives.

Unlike in Britain, the party has no titular leader. Presently, none of the four most significant elected posts in Washington – those of president, vice president, House speaker and Senate majority leader – are occupied by a Democrat. Elders such as Bill and Hillary Clinton and Barack Obama occasionally enter the political fray. But the party lacks a talismanic figure or pre-eminent standard-bearer. Up against a colossal and omnipresent figure like Trump, high-ranking Democrats have often looked like lightweights. Or bit players lacking central character energy.

Can you recall a moment, for instance, when the party’s Senate leader, Chuck Schumer, landed a glove on the President?

Does the name Hakeem Jeffries even ring a bell? If the Democrats regain control of the House of Representatives in next month’s midterm elections, the 56-year-old Congressman will become the first African-American House speaker in US history. Yet he could hardly be described as a leader of the opposition. After Jeffries suggested that his fellow Democrats sit in “silent defiance” during Trump’s State of the Union address in February, late-night host Stephen Colbert pilloried him for coming up with what he called “a bold brand of doing jack squat.” Then, mercilessly, Colbert compared him with Black leaders from the past. “As Martin Luther King once said,” the comedian deadpanned, “‘Sh-h-h’”. 

Ahead of the midterms, Jeffries has become more vocal. “Operation Epic Failure” is how he, like so many others, describes “Operation Epic Fury”, the war with Iran which has driven up fuel and grocery prices. Still, Jeffries has been unable to shrug off the criticism voiced most strongly by local activists in his home district of Brooklyn, who heckled him with the chant: “Grow a spine.”

Not all Democrats have been flat-lining. California Governor Gavin Newsom, ahead of his probable bid for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028, frequently shirtfronts the President. Last week, after Trump blithely spoke of Iran wiping out Los Angeles and San Diego, he denounced the President as “deranged and dangerous” and called for the cabinet and Congress to invoke the 25th Amendment, which allows for the removal of a president unable to discharge his duties (spoiler alert, this will never happen because the cabinet is packed with sycophants and because it requires two-thirds votes in both chambers of Congress).

Left-wing firebrand Bernie Sanders can still pack out a stadium rally, which he has been doing since the start of Trump 2.0, alongside protégé, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, in their nationwide Fighting Oligarchy Tour. It says a lot about the sorry state of the Democratic Party, though, that one of its most effective pugilists is a snowy-haired 85-year-old, who was first elected to Congress 36 years ago, when AOC had just celebrated her first birthday.

As Congresswoman Ocasio-Cortez reminds us, the party is not completely devoid of talented up-and-comers. Georgia Senator John Ossoff, who is fighting a tough battle for re-election in one of the country’s key battleground states, instantly made a name for himself when, during a rally in August, he accused Trump of being preoccupied with home improvements at the White House, and his presidential aide Natalie Harp. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani is a gifted political communicator, especially fluent on TikTok. But Mamdani made his name attacking a fellow Democrat, former New York governor Andrew Cuomo, in last year’s mayoral primary, rather than Trump.

That “Big Apple” contest pitted a left-wing populist, Mamdani, against an establishment centrist, Cuomo, and was billed as a battle for the soul of the Democratic Party. This ideological fight has consumed the party ever since it lost to a felonious former president who many expected to end up in a federal penitentiary with iron bars rather than a federal mansion with gold trappings. The midterms, which will probably result in victories for moderates and left-wingers alike, are unlikely to resolve this argument. 

Rather than philosophising about the future direction of the party, the Democrats should be focused on the political here and now. Why have they not made more, for instance, of the Trump family gaining so much financially since its billionaire patriarch was restored to the White House, especially at a time when cost of living pressures bear down on average Americans?

Few things speak more of the failure of other senior Democrats to achieve cut-through than the fact Kamala Harris, the former vice president who lost the 2024 election, is currently front-runner in the race for the party’s 2028 presidential nomination. But that could soon change, especially if Ossoff wins in Georgia. So far this 39-year-old, who has a master’s degree from the London School of Economics, has been the standout performer of the 2026 electoral cycle.

Whether through accident or design, the Carville “play dead” strategy looks like reaping a rich harvest. The Democrats are poised to win back control of the House of Representatives, where they need a net gain of just three seats (midway through Trump’s first term, the party made a net gain of 40 seats). The party could also wrest back control of the Senate, which seemed unthinkable at the start of the year because so many races are in states such as Ohio, Texas, Iowa and Kansas, where Trump won comfortably in 2024.

If they do win back both houses of Congress, Democrats will be able to investigate more rigorously the Trump administration with subpoena powers that come with a majority. They could impeach the President for a third time, although they will not have the votes to win a conviction in the ensuing Senate trial. Victory in November would surely signal an end to their zombification. On Capitol Hill, we might witness the return of the living dead.

news.title: Comment on KAMALA HARRIS : CE QU’ON LUI REPROCHE QUAND ELLE ÉTAIT PROCUREURE by space waves
news.text:
Dans mon boulot, je rencontre beaucoup de personnes qui ont des parcours migratoiresdifférents : des Indiens, des Pakistanais, des Chinois, des Russes, des Ukrainiens, desAfghans, des Turcs, des personnes d’Amérique latine, des Africains.Dans tout ceci, il y a une question qui me revient et est posée par les Africains : Pourquoi es-tuautant dur avec nous ?

À la Vice-Présidente Kamara, nos frères Afro-Américains lui posent aussi la même question :Pourquoi es-tu si dure envers nous quand tu étais procureure ?

À cette question, il y a une réponse toute simple qui sauve celles et ceux qui la posent et aussinotre communauté.

Nul n’ignore qu’aux Etats-Unis, les Afro-américains sont d’abord laissés dans la précarité qui lesforce à commettre des petits délits. Les petits délits les conduisent en prison ensuite. Etpuisque leur casier judiciaire est chargé, ils ont du mal à se réinsérer dans la vie et le cycle desdélits, de la prison et de la précarité continue finalement.

Aux Etats-Unis aussi, les Afro-Américains sont des minorités. La police en majorité blanche estune institution extrêmement solide, respectée, crainte et aimée par tous et surtout la majorité.

Que reproche une partie de la communauté noire à Kamala ?Certains de nos compatriotes la qualifient de “redoutable et sans pitié.” comme le souligneDavid Vauclair.Certains Africains l’accusent aussi d’avoir refusé ” que l’on poursuive des policiers qui avaientété accusés de violences”.“En 2014, elle va refuser d’enquêter sur la mort de deux Afro-Américains qui sont abattus par lapolice. En 2015, elle ne soutiendra pas un projet de loi qui obligeait le procureur général, elle àl’époque, à nommer un procureur qui se spécialise dans la poursuite judiciaire des violencespolicières” David Vauclair

Je ne sais pas si nos compatriotes savent vraiment lire le monde dans lequel nous sommes ets’ils savent que la lutte de reconnaissance que notre peuple mène n’est pas une lutte de 5jours, de cent jours, de 1000 jours, mais une lutte de tous les jours.

Comme je l’ai écrit tantôt, la police est une institution forte aux Etats-Unis. Kamara était unesimple procureure et si elle condamnait ces policiers en ce moment précis, elle monterait toutela police contre notre peuple. Elle donnerait aussi du grain à moudre au politicien raciste etpopuliste comme Trump. Elle serait déposée, eu le même sort qui était réservé à notrecompatriote Claudine Gay de Harvard.On a l’exemple vu de France où les manifestations contre les policiers ont fait monter lapopularité de Zemmour et des Le Pen.Hier, s’il n’y avait pas eu le compatriote Jean-Luc qui est de tous les combats pour le vivreensemble, le Front national aurait pris le pouvoir.Aux Etats-Unis, Obama était président (pas un simple procureur) et n’avait rien pu faire contreles violences policières. Ces larmes n’y ont rien changé.

C’est pourquoi Kamala a adopté la meilleure stratégie : être dure avec ses sœurs et frères.

Pour protéger les petits délinquants précarisés et les faire sortir du cycle de l’emprisonnement,la procureure Harris les maintient un peu plus longtemps en prison afin qu’ils bénéficient mieuxdes programmes de réinsertion.“Back on Track”, en 2005 était son initiative. “Ce programme de retour sur les rails lui a permisde réduire les taux de récidive en Californie de 70% à 10%. news.title: The $2500 Donation that could mean more for Texas' Senate race than Elon Musk’s millions
news.text:
Barbara Bush, the daughter of former President George W. Bush, has given money to a super PAC supporting Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, Houston Public Media reported.

The amount is small, but it may say something about where some Republicans stand.

Lone Star Rising PAC’s third-quarter filing with the FEC lists a $2,500 contribution from the younger Bush, dated September 23. The Bush family didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Andrew Cates, a campaign finance attorney in central Texas, noted that someone from such a prominent family could easily have given in a way that kept her name out of public view. Instead, he said, she chose a PAC that discloses all of its money, not a 501(c)(4) that would have kept her donation anonymous.

He said the sum is minor in a race that has drawn hundreds of millions of dollars.

“It’s not like Elon Musk money, obviously,” Cates said.

Still, he suggested the gift could hint at where the moderate Republican establishment is leaning and how it sees the contest ending.

Polls show Talarico and Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton roughly tied, or with Talarico narrowly ahead.

Barbara Bush already made clear her willingness to back Democrats two years ago, when she supported then-Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 election.

news.title: How Latino Voters Are Experiencing the 2026 Midterm Elections - Pew Research Center
news.text:
Several weeks out from the 2026 midterm election, Democratic congressional candidates have a sizable advantage among Latino registered voters. And while not all registered voters will cast ballots this year, Latino Democratic candidate supporters are more engaged with this year’s election compared with four years ago.

77% of Latino registered voters who support a Democratic candidate for their district in the House of Representatives say it really matters who wins control of Congress, up from 58% in 2022.

53% say they’re extremely motivated to vote, up from 41% four years ago.

45% say they’ve given a lot of thought to the upcoming elections, up from 24% in 2022.

Meanwhile, Latino voters who support Republican congressional candidates show lower levels of engagement this year compared with Latino voters supporting Democratic candidates.

Latino registered voters overall are more engaged in this year’s election than they were at a similar point before the 2022 midterms. Their current level of interest is similar to other registered voters. By contrast, in 2022, Latino voters were less engaged than other voters.

Latino voters have historically favored Democratic over Republican candidates in midterm elections, but the margin has narrowed in recent years: In 2022, Latino voters backed Democrats over Republicans by a 21 percentage point margin, down from a 47-point margin in 2018. Trump also made gains among Latino voters in presidential elections between 2016 and 2024, winning nearly half their votes two years ago. Previous Pew Research Center studies have found that differences in who turns out to vote, rather than voters switching their support between parties, have played a role in these shifts.

Two years into the second Trump administration, the president’s standing with Latino voters has deteriorated. His current job approval rating among Latino voters, at 24%, is down from 38% in February 2025. And majorities of Latino voters say the Trump administration’s policies harm Hispanics more than help them and that their situation as a group is worse than a year ago. (Jump to “Trump’s falling job approval rating among Latino registered voters.”)

The economy remains the top issue for Latino voters, who have grown more negative about economic conditions and are increasingly concerned about the cost of gas and unemployment. (Jump to “The Economy Is the Top Issue for Latino Voters in the 2026 Midterms.”)

These findings come from a new Pew Research Center survey of U.S. adults, including 774 Hispanic registered voters, conducted from Sept. 28 to Oct. 4, 2026.

Vote preferences among Hispanic voters in the 2026 midterm elections

Democrats hold a 27 percentage point advantage over Republicans among all Hispanic registered voters in the national race for the House of Representatives – 51% to 24%. Another 18% say they are not sure who they would vote for, and an additional 7% indicate they would support another candidate.

According to the new survey, 65% of Hispanic voters who voted for Trump in 2024 say they support the Republican House candidate this year. Another 14% say they would vote for another candidate, 11% say they would vote for the Democratic candidate, and 10% say they’re not sure whom they would vote for.

Meanwhile, 84% of Hispanic voters who supported Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024 say they back the Democratic House candidate this year.

Among those who did not vote in 2024, 47% say they would choose the Democratic candidate and 18% the Republican candidate. An additional 31% say they are unsure who they would vote for, while 4% favor another candidate.

For more information, visit the detailed tables on voting preferences and presidential approval. 

(Jump to “Latino Registered Voters See the Democratic Party More Favorably Than the Republican Party.”)

For many Latino voters, Trump is a factor in their congressional vote choices

A majority of Latino registered voters (55%) say they think of their vote for Congress this fall as a vote against Trump. Another 14% say their vote is in support of him, while 30% say he is not much of a factor.

This is a substantial change from four years ago, when 26% of Latino voters viewed their vote as support for Joe Biden and 23% viewed it as opposition to him. About half (48%) said he was not a factor in their congressional vote choice. 

Hispanic voters who back a Republican candidate are about equally likely to say their vote for Congress is a vote for Trump or that Trump is not much of a factor for their vote (46% each). Only 7% say they think about their vote as a vote against Trump.

A strong majority (84%) of Hispanic voters who say they support a Democratic candidate for Congress this year view their vote as opposition to Trump. And 14% say Trump is not a factor in their vote for Congress.

Among Hispanic voters who backed Trump in 2024, 35% say their vote for Congress this year is a vote for the president. Yet 19% view their vote as opposition to Trump. Another 46% say he is not much of a factor in their vote choice.

Trump’s falling job approval rating among Latino registered voters

Today, 24% of Latino registered voters say they approve of Trump’s handling of his job as president. This number has fallen 14 percentage points from the start of his second term, when 38% approved of his job.

The president’s job approval rating has fallen more sharply among his 2024 Hispanic voters. At the start of his second term, 93% said they approved of his job as president. Now, 57% say this – a decline of 36 percentage points. Approval has also fallen among Trump’s 2024 non-Hispanic backers, though less sharply. In February 2025, 95% approved of his job performance, compared with 68% today.

The impact of Trump’s policies on Hispanics

Seven-in-ten Hispanic registered voters (70%) say the Trump administration’s policies have been harmful to Hispanics, while 12% say they have been helpful and 16% say they have had no effect. This is similar to their assessment from a year ago, when 74% said the administration’s policies were harmful to Hispanics. 

Today, views differ sharply by how Hispanic registered voters say they will vote in the House election:

Republican candidate supporters are divided: 23% say the administration’s policies have been harmful, while 37% say they have been helpful. Another 38% say they have had no effect.

Almost all Democratic candidate supporters say the administration’s policies have been harmful to Hispanics (91%).

How Hispanic voters view the situation of Hispanics in the country

About six-in-ten Hispanic registered voters (61%) say the situation of Hispanics in the United States is worse than it was a year ago, while 11% say it is better and 26% say it is about the same.

The share who say Latinos’ situation in the U.S. is worse than a year ago is roughly the same as the share that said this a year ago (65%).

However, the reference periods differ. This year’s assessment asks respondents to compare the situation today with the first year of Trump’s second administration. Last year, they were comparing the first year of Trump’s second administration to the final year of the Biden administration.

This year’s negative assessment of Hispanics’ situation remains far above previous years: In 2021, only 28% said Hispanics’ situation had worsened in the previous year, and in 2019, 42% said this. 

Hispanic registered voters’ choice of congressional candidate this year is related to how they see the situation of U.S. Hispanics.

Hispanic Republican candidate supporters are divided: 22% say the situation of Hispanics is worse than a year ago, while 34% say it’s better and 44% say it’s about the same.

On the other hand, 79% of Democratic candidate supporters say the situation of Hispanics is worse than a year ago, while only 2% say it’s better and 19% say it’s about the same.
news.summary: How Latino Voters Are Experiencing the 2026 Midterm Elections - Pew Research Center
